utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in and around the courtroom. Could we please call the case, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, and good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-81-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Perisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Could we have the appearances for the day, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, counsel, everyone in the courtroom. Mark Harmon, Salvatore Cannata, and Carmela Javier for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everybody in the courtroom. Appearing for Mr. Perisic today are Boris Zorko, Tina Drolec, and Novak Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Good morning, Mr. Novakovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Novakovic. You know what I'm going to be saying, that you've taken the declaration to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing else but the truth. Thank you so much. Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good morning, General Novakovic.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: At the end of the session, we ran out of time, but you had asked to see a document that -- and which I had reviewed with you paragraphs 11 and 12. So let me call that document up to the screen because you wanted to refer to paragraph 2 of that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could I have 65 ter 5989 on the screen, please. Could we - let me see - go to the first page in the English, please. I'd like to display paragraph 2. It's probably the first page of the Serbian-language version as well. No, it's not that page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You can see the bottom of page 2 -- paragraph 2 in this, General. We will turn the page so you can see the next page as well after you have a chance to review the first portion of paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If we could turn to --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Have you had a chance to review paragraph 2?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could we turn to the next page in the Serbian language.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, I believe that that was the preceding documents that you quoted extensive passages from and not this one, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Sorry, I did not get a translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you sure you're on the same -- the correct channel, number 4, channel 4?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have a slight problem with my plug here. It wasn't -- okay. I can read the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Then we will change to the other document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could I have Prosecution Exhibit 2919 on the monitor, please. And, again, I would like the first page of the English, and it is undoubtedly the first page of the Serbian version as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. General, you see in front of you paragraph 2. It comes in under the section of "Violations of the Cease-Fire." Is that the section you wanted to review and comment on?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No verbal response]

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You have to answer audibly, sir.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Then if we could -- for the witness, can you then go to the next page in the Serbian language so he can review -- actually, that's the section I think that the witness wanted to comment on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Sir, what is your comment in respect of paragraph 2 of this document?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be useful for me if I were to have this in front of my eyes, Mr. Harmon. I apologise. That would be on the preceding page, the one that you showed just earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Is that -- it should -- it appears now on the screen. The preceding page is on the monitor. Yes, sir. I invite your comment.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, thank you for your effort, Mr. Harmon, for allowing me to see this. I need this because you said - and by that you started that part of your intervention - that my statement was false, that the area of the Republic of Serbian Krajina was demilitarised and that that claim was false because there existed paramilitary forces called "posebne," or special units, of police. Here and now I would like to responding [as interpreted] to your thesis. Special units of police were what today are anti-terrorist units, which means for each such unit in the world which are specialised for performing such tasks may in a sense be regarded as paramilitary if that term, "paramilitary," encompasses their purpose, their equipment, their training, and the character of tasks that they perform. My claim, and I repeat it, is this: Special units of police were part and parcel of the regular forces of police in the Republic of Serbian Krajina, that is, in the UN protected areas. Realistic -- in accordance with realistic needs and the forms of threats to the population, they were structured in the same way that police forces are structured around the world when taken into account the character of threat to the population. Mr. Harmon, you may know -- now say that in this document it is stated that these are such forces. But let's take things one at a time. For instance, in paragraph 2 it reads, in the row 3 in the Serbian language: "However, tension has been high in Sector South, particularly in the areas of the Peruca Dam, the Miljevci Plateau," and this is characteristic only in brackets, Mr. Harmon, "(where there was a Croatian army incursion on the 21st of June 1992) and Zemunik Airport; in these areas, heavy machine-guns and light mortars have sometimes been used." My thesis stays, Mr. Harmon, that in conditions where UNPROFOR deployed in companies, in camps, encircled with wire with couple of check-points along roads which control nobody and nothing, means that anybody who is responsible for the security of the population in an area should have sufficient force that would prevent such conduct or events. I'm going to continue with the page 3. If you allow me, let me focus --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Sir, if you could concentrate your mind and just distill what you wanted to say very briefly. I don't want to spend an enormous amount of time on this. You've testified earlier that one of the reasons these forces existed was to prevent and to protect the Serbian population from Croatian incursions. That is in your testimony on direct examination. You've made that point. Do you have anything else, any other point you'd like to make in respect of paragraph 2?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could you do so succinctly, please.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Referring to this document, you treat it as a judgement, as if it were a document whereby a panel of judges has determined the facts beyond reasonable doubt. And this is how you treat that document, this is how you see it. However, Mr. Harmon, this is a political document par excellence. Therefore, between it and a possible judgement, there is a huge chasm, there is a huge difference. And I'm invoking paragraph 2 to illustrate that. You see the words "where there's been an incursion of the Croatian army on 21st of June, 1992," is put in brackets. It doesn't say that 40 people were killed, that their bodies were thrown into ravines, and many of them have never been found. You think this is insignificant? What I mean: Such documents reflect the relationship and the relations of power in political sense, and these are documents which try to balance out political power, which means some things are emphasised, some things are interpreted in a certain way, certain marginal things come to the fore, and some important things become marginalised. And this is what I illustrate on the basis of paragraph 2. If you allow me, let's go to paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Sir, paragraph 3 speaks for itself. It identifies a number of major incidents, as characterised, in which Serbs were the victims of Croatian incursions. That's what paragraph 3 reflects. That is what this document reports to the Security Council. This document is a report to the Security Council. And if you have -- I don't want to go into detail on each one of these incidents that's described, or any other incidents. Have you concluded, sir, then your comments in respect of paragraph 2?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, with respect to paragraph 2, I've finished my comments, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, sir. Now, what I would like to do very succinctly and quickly with you, General Novakovic, is have you affirm the following facts for me. I will explain the fact to you -- in fact, General, on -- when the Territorial Defence and the special police units in approximately November of 1992 -- when the -- let me rephrase the question. When the SVK was reorganised in November of 1992, the special police units were absorbed into the SVK, were they not?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. Harmon. But you have not allowed me to comment on the thesis concerning the falsehood of my claims about the events with General Nambiar and Mr. Goulding. But, however, the answer to this question is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Can you comment on the claim -- can you comment on what we discussed with -- what you testified to in -- with General Nambiar and Marrack Goulding? Can you do that succinctly, sir? Apparently you want to make a comment on your previous testimony. Can you do that succinctly?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No verbal response]

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I can't hear -- I need to have an audible answer for the record. You have to say either yes or no. If you shake your head up and down, the court reporter can't record that.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay, okay. Would you then comment succinctly, sir, on what you want to say about General Nambiar and Marrack Goulding.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, Mr. Harmon, it is first and foremost in my best interest to provide succinct answers because I'm growing weary. You did not believe that Mr. Goulding was positively -- has had a positive attitude with respect to the demilitarisation of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. I remember very well that after the meeting with Mr. Marrack Goulding in Knin that we were in a euphoric state because finally somebody said something positive about what we said. What happened between Knin and Jurik [phoen] when this report was finally presented, I don't know. But I can tell you what I remember quite well. If I were to have something that I do not know and I don't need, a team, then I would be able to show you General Nambiar's interviews after his mandate was finished --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: General Novakovic, just tell us exactly what happened between you and General Nambiar. You've talked now for about ten lines and you have still not told us enough of what happened between you and Mr. Nambiar. Why were you -- Why did the meeting end in euphoria? What happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I previously said, Your Honours, that General Nambiar had no objections to the conduct of the Serbian side in the implementation of the Vance Plan. Mr. Harmon --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You see, you have told us that in your evidence in chief. Mr. Harmon has shown you reports that state the contrary. Now, you are supposed to comment on the reports that state the contrary, to show that what you are saying is correct and not what the report contains. And that's what Mr. Harmon is giving you a chance to do. Please tell us that without repeating what you told us in evidence in chief.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can only supplement that I know well that after leaving the mandate, General Nambiar gave interviews to international media which reflect what he told us in personal contacts, and that was that the Serbian side, as opposed to the other side, supported and implemented the Vance Plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, let me return to the topic I was discussing with you, which was the absorption of the special police units into the SVK. What I'd like you to do is confirm the following information, if you would: The 80th Special Police Unit, of which you were commander, was incorporated into the 21st Corps, was it not?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And did it retain the same designation that it had? In other words, when it was incorporated into the 21st Corps, was it a unit that remained intact and was called the special police unit, or did it have another designation?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 80th Brigade of Special Units of Police ceased to exist as a unit. The men from those units, in accordance with their skills, were deployed into the units of the 21st Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the 75th Special Police Unit from Knin and the 92nd Special Police Unit from Benkovac were absorbed into the 7th Corps; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those units did not enter, but the men entered those units based on their competences for military service in the area -- in the units which were established in Northern Dalmatia, and that would be the 7th Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the men who were in the 79th Special Police Unit in Korenica were absorbed into the Lika Corps; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were accepted into the units of the Lika Corps, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Men of the 83rd Special Police Units from Petrinje were absorbed into the 39th Corps; do you affirm that?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can confirm that. I can confirm for all the other units of special units of police that in their areas of responsibility were disbanded, and their men, as such, entered units of the newly established SVK. That's correct. That's what I can confirm.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let me -- just for the record, so it's complete, that would include: The 85th Special Police from Okucani were absorbed into the 18th Corps; the 87th Special Police from Vukovar were absorbed into the 11th Corps; and the men from the 90th Special Police Unit in Beli Manastir were absorbed into the 11th Corps. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Men from those units, but units as such were disbanded just as in every other zone or area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could I have a Defence -- let me see. Just one minute. I may have the wrong exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could I have Defence Exhibit 442 MFI on the monitor, please. While we're waiting for the document to come up, could I have the last exhibit admitted into evidence; it's 65 ter 5989.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Exhibit 5989 is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P2920.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Sir, this is an entry from the -- General Mladic's diary from -- of a meeting that took place on the 8th of November, 1993. You reviewed this with Defence counsel in proofing and testified extensively about it in the course of your evidence in chief. This is the meeting at which the Drina Plan was ordered to be prepared by President Milosevic, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not understand what kind of plan you meant, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I meant the plan that ultimately became known as the Drina Plan. You testified -- you testified earlier about a portion of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are receiving a slightly different interpretation into Serbian. Mr. Harmon is referring to the Drina Plan. So that the witness is not confused.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I get the interpretation "Drinski" Plan instead of "Drina" plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I haven't heard of that plan yet, so it's the Drina Plan is what I'm referring to, sir. So this is where -- this is the meeting. As you can see, you attended. You can see the people who were present. It was a large number of people in the political hierarchy in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, of the RSK, and of the RS, as well as military leaders from those entities. There was a significant number of attendees. And it was at that meeting that Mr. Milosevic said to start compiling a single war plan and define how to continue waging the war, a single plan for all of the three armies. I just want you to confirm that this is the meeting where that took place?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I guess he said -- he confirmed that in chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Well, then, I want to move to a different element of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Sir, if I could turn to - just get the right page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If I could turn to page -- the next page in the English version. And if I could turn to -- I think it's the next page in the Serbian-language version as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you see in your language, sir, a section that says "Our Objective"? Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. You'll see a section that says - and you testified -- you testified about this section in your evidence in chief. You didn't testify about a line, however, in the section that says: "The basic precondition ..." The last line before the items that are asterisked says: "Break sanctions in every way possible." Do you see that? Is that in your language version? Then it should be on the -- do you see that? If not, we'll go to the next page, sir, in the Serbian language.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. That's fine. That's all I would -- okay. Tell -- can you, please --

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it, Mr. Harmon. But I don't know whether that's what it says in English. There are two lines at the beginning of the paragraph, and it doesn't say "the basic objective" but "the basic concept" or "idea."

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, do you -- I want to focus your attention, General, on the line that says --

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the sanctions, it says --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It says: "Break sanctions in every way possible" in the translation that I have. You attended that meeting. What does that refer to, sir? What do you recall from that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With regard to the minutes of the meeting, I remember from the meeting that Mr. Milosevic spoke about the economic sanctions which had been imposed on the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and I remember well that he said that the existence of sanctions was an ideal environment for trade of all kind. Instead of you seeking to buy weapons, people from all over the world come to you to sell it to you. And I remember that that was exactly what Mr. Milosevic said with regard to what is noted here, to break sanctions in every way. I believe that Mr. Milosevic was even in a good mood when he proffered that comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me turn to page 25 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And it's also 25 in the Serbian-language version. Fine. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You see, I want to direct your attention to the comment next to number 10. It says: "Rakic (RSK MO ..." You told us he was the minister of defence. He was an admiral, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harmon, he was an admiral --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And he was --

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and he was also the minister of defence of the Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you know who paid his salary?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who paid his salary, but there is no reason for me not to believe that it was the ministry of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, he makes a comment, and I want you to discuss with us your recollection of this comment and what was meant by it. His comment is: "Our army is destitute ..." And I take it, first of all, he's referring to the SVK. Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And, sir, tell us what Admiral Rakic was discussing in respect of that entry.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Admiral Rakic spoke -- what I had always stated at our requests for co-ordination, and that was that our situation was disastrous, that we didn't have anything, and that those who were always in trenches, those soldiers were in the worst situation. They didn't have boots, they didn't have uniforms, there was not enough food. And I remember perfectly at the time, Mr. Harmon, a detail that can be a good illustration of the situation: Even when there was food, there were no spices; and even if food was prepared and given to the troops, they would not eat it because it was not spicy, it didn't taste good. And that's what Admiral Rakic meant when he said what he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Why was Admiral Rakic raising the destitute condition of the SVK at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, he believed that people around him were influential, that they were decision-makers who could improve the situation. At that time, the most important influential and political authority was Mr. Milosevic, and he was there, as well as members of the leadership of Serbia, not the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia but Serbia. And those were people who could be instrumental in improving the financial and materiel situation of the Army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When you say those were people who could improve the financial and materiel situation of the Army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, are you referring to those are the people who would be in a position to provide the SVK with ammunition, for example, with tank companies, with artillery pieces, with materiel that's necessary for the standard functioning of an army?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we are still talking about what the minister of defence of the Army of Srpska Krajina said, that didn't imply war equipment and materiel but other types of materiel. And what he expected from political authorities was to make a decision and for the Government of the Republic of Serbia together with the Government of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, obviously who had not invested a lot of effort into that, to find a practical solution to that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You mentioned the types of materiel in your earlier answer: Not enough food, not enough boots, not enough uniforms. What other types of materiels was General -- Admiral Rakic referring to that the SVK needed to acquire in order to function as an army?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that meeting, Admiral Rakic dealt with those issues that were primarily within his remit. In addition to the quartermaster's equipment, Mr. Harmon, as we call it - and you said it yourself that those were boots and uniforms and foodstuffs - primarily that's the fuel and lubricants for the normal functioning of the Army of Republic of Serbian Krajina. We needed 800 to 1.000 tonnes a month. It's not much, but still we didn't have that. Moreover, there was a problem with spare parts. Also a problem with medical supplies. There was a problem with repairs of our vehicles and the use of overall resources.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Without that type of materiel, could the SVK have functioned as an army?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the situation as it was and without all that, we managed to function in one way or another, Mr. Harmon. But the situation deteriorated, and it was only a matter of time how long we could go on. And the consequences of -- were not suffered only by the troops and how many pieces of artillery they were ready to launch in a minute, but also there was a question of the soldiers' morale.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. The issue on soldiers' morale is: Without having sufficient provisions, their morale deteriorated and that impacted on whether they were willing to continue to serve in the SVK; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, Mr. Harmon. Unfortunately, there were men who were weaker than others, and they left the territory of the Republic of Serbian Krajina and their army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Go on, sir.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. I mean people from Krajina, those who were born and raised there and who resided there at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, General, the next entry is your entry. It says: "We need two tank companies and one division for Eastern Slavonia ..." And then there are ellipses, suggesting that you continued and you had a lot more to say than that. What do you recall the issues you raised at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on the command of the 11th Corps and my insight into the situation, in order to cover the entire front line, the support artillery which was meant to provide support to the defence, and in order to have some sort of manoeuvre force in the second line, I proffered a realistic military assessment. I thought that we needed those things, and that's what I requested.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And did you request any ammunition, any artillery pieces, beside tanks? Did you request any other sort of materiel at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was just the basic requirement. I always repeated my requirements. I must have been wearing people out. I always repeated that our equipment was exhausted, our ammunition was exhausted; and always repeated those requests with regard to the equipment and materiel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness said, I always repeated those requests and I'm sure that I -- that people found me boring. And that was not recorded. That was never mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you say that, sir? Can you confirm that that's what you said?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did you not say you were wearing people out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I said that most probably my requests were wearing people out, that people found me boring as a result of my requests.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We're going to return to this document in just one minute, but I'd like -- before, could I have Prosecution Exhibit 2175 on the stand, and I want English e-court 0630-5913, B/C/S page 23 on the monitor. Yes, this is the page. Sir, on -- you were -- you commented on this in your case in chief, particularly -- and I'm referring you to sub-part 3, the provision of fuel and other propellants. And you were asked: "Did you, as the SVK, receive oil and fuel from the VJ?" And this document, which is dated the -- I'll just find the date on this. This date -- this is the 23rd of September, 1993. You were asked --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Where do we find that date, Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We find it, Your Honour -- I've noted it, but let me find the date. Just bear with me for one minute. Your Honour, the date is found on ET 06 -- 0630-5902 ET. This was a document -- this portion that I've referred to is a small portion of a large document. The larger document is entitled: "Topics for discussion of the Chief of the General Staff of the VJ with commanders of the Main Staffs of the Serbian Army of Krajina and Republika Srpska." And in brackets underneath that is a date, the 23rd of September, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, I see you tried to give us that page, but you gave us 5905 instead of 5902 -- oh, okay. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And in the English version, Your Honour, you'll see it at the top, under the caption --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: -- that's the date --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: -- of the document. And the part that I've referred to which is -- if we could then return to ET -- 0630-5913 ET, that is a sub-part of this larger document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, sir, you testified in respect of this document. You were asked the question: "Did you, as the SVK, receive oil and fuel from the VJ?" And your answer at 13191, starting at line 1, you said: "I don't know whether there was anything before this document, but after that for sure nothing else came. They themselves did not have enough fuel to meet their everyday minimum requirements."

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, if we could turn back to Defence Exhibit 442 MFI, I'd like to go to page 26 of the English and the Serbian-language version. Could I have -- there we go. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, at this meeting on the 8th of November, 1993, President Milosevic says the following: "The army must be a priority. "1.000 tonnes of fuel must go to the RSK." You see that passage, sir, next to the number 14?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, I can see that, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So after the 23rd of September, did you receive this thousand tonnes of fuel?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Did you receive -- in addition to that 1.000 tonnes of fuel, did you receive other allotments of fuel from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I was in command, certain quantities did arrive but not as much as necessary. In September, on the 9th of September, at the time of this document, the strategic reserves of the fuel in possession of the Serbian Republic of Krajina army were 27.000 litres, just one tank. And 3 tonnes were assigned to an armoured battalion. But now you should ask me where that fuel came from in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me deal with my examination the way I would like to, General Novakovic. First of all, in September -- you said: "... on the 9th of September, at the time of this document ..." --

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: -- this document was the 23rd of September, not the 9th -- okay? Now, address your question, where this fuel came from. Where did this thousand tonnes of fuel that President Milosevic sent to the RSK, where did that come from?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, I was not involved in fuel. It was the Ministry of Defence, the prime minister, and my assistant for logistics who were dealing with fuel. That fuel was obtained in the following way: Raw oil from Djeletovci in the eastern part of the Republic of Serbian Krajina was sent to the refinery in Pancevo, and from there we received a certain quantity of oil products. And that's what I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, could we take a look at Defence Exhibit 441, please, MFI 441. And I'd like to go, first of all, to the first page so we can just see the date on this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This meeting is -- you recall, sir, is a meeting you attended in Belgrade on the 21st of October, 1993. It was attended by the people who are identified on the first page. You testified --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If we could turn to the next page, please, in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I just want to show you a portion of this document. There's a portion to the bottom of your page that says "questions," and I just want you to refresh your recollection with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, on this page, it's -- toward the bottom of the page, it says "questions."

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And this is the portion of your evidence where you said that two units were transferred from the VRS to the Lika Corps. You identified General Boric and General Talic as being VRS generals. And that, in fact, they sent to Eastern Slavonia -- sorry, they sent two units, two battalions, 500 men each, to the SVK. Do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, this confirms that a unit from Eastern Slavonia was dispatched. I said that commanders of the 1st and 2nd Krajina Corps, Generals Boric and Talic, sent one battalion each, up to 500 men, to Lika for periods of up to one month.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's correct. I thought I had summarised that. Perhaps I didn't summarise it accurately. But you have summarised your previous testimony accurately. Now, the question I have, sir: When the VRS troops came into the area of responsibility of the SVK, did they continue to wear their VRS insignia?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly switch off unnecessary mikes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So they were operating in your theatre of operations with VRS uniforms and VRS insignia, indicating that they were from the 1st Krajina Corps and the 2nd Krajina Corps of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harmon. I'm sure that not all of them wore insignia. That was the state of their uniforms. But those who had them wore them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And was UNPROFOR operating in the area of responsibility where the two battalions from the VRS had come?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not understand your question. What do you mean when you say "the area of responsibility." What is the area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You said that two battalions of VRS soldiers came into the SVK territory. Was UNPROFOR also operating in the same territory where the VRS units had come?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Can you tell -- explain to me how President Milosevic could say and order that the VRS send troops to the SVK and that that order was executed. Can you explain to me how that took place, how that's possible?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic could not issue an order to that effect. It was his suggestion. And in the minutes, it says for Boric and Talic to assist them. If it had been an order, it would have been recorded differently. It would have been recorded in this way: I hereby order that commanders of the 1st, 2nd, and 3rd Krajina Corps by this date send so many men at such and such time, and those units shall be resubordinated to so and so. That would have been an order. This is a suggestion. Mr. Milosevic thought that units from Eastern Slavonia should not be dispatched, given the fact that the 1st and 2nd Krajina Corps zones are in contact with the zones where the problems arose. That was a time when the Medacki Dzep situation arose. Let me remind you, Mr. Harmon, of the fact that Republika Srpska and the Republic of Serbian Krajina were being merged or united at least three times.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, the entry says that by 27 October, 1993 - and this is on the third page of this entry - two brigades equal about 3.000 men to be given to the RSK to Lika. That's the way the entry reads. And the person who proposed that solution was President Milosevic, and that solution was executed. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Harmon. I'm telling you that suggestion was not implemented. It was suggested here that 3- to 5.000 men be sent; however, it didn't amount to even 1.000 men. And just for a three- to four-week period that they stayed there. And those men who, because of an increase of intensity and tensions after the Medak Dzep incursion, those men could, after that, be given an opportunity for some R and R to go home and rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Could we --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could we take a look at Prosecution Exhibit 317.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We're going to be taking a look, sir, at your evidence in respect of the Drina Plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And if we could turn to page 3 of the English in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, sir, this was the aide-memoire for the co-ordination of tasks of the VJ General Staff on 17 December 1993, and your attention during your evidence in chief was directed to passages that relate to number 1: "Analysis of the implementation of tasks from the previous co-ordination ..." And then it had: "(a) implemented tasks: Plans for the use of the troops have been fully developed up to the corps level." And you were asked by Mr. Lukic what had been achieved up to the corps level in terms of the implementation. And your answer was, and I quote: "After a joint war plan had been drafted, we updated our war plan at the Main Staff level to the extent necessary by the modifications of the joint war plan and its schedules, meaning the entirety of the joint war plan. However, at the corps level and lower, we did not draft the war plan."

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Your Honours, the only cite I have -- I didn't have the official transcript cite for that answer, but it's the LiveNote at page 38, lines 11 through 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, early, sir, we looked at the Defence Exhibit 442 MFI, which was the Mladic diary entry, where general -- President Milosevic suggested, in the presence of numerous political and military leaders, that a war plan be created. Your evidence was -- is to the effect that at a lower level from the corps you didn't develop those war plans. My question to you, sir, is: Did you at any time inform the attendees at the meeting of the 8th of November, including General Perisic, General Mladic, political leaders, that you had not developed the war plan at the lower echelons, the echelons below the corps level?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that is how my, then, answer is understood - I don't know how it's reflected in English - well then it is partly inaccurate, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, I have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not understand the question, Mr. Harmon, as asked. And I listened to it in the Serbian language and I'm looking at it in the English language. I would like the witness to leave the courtroom for a moment, please, to explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, Mr. Lukic asks that you excuse us for a short while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What Mr. Harmon is referring to is 17th of December, 1993, co-ordination of tasks meeting. That's the reference. The meeting was held on the 8th of November, 1993; and the Drina Plan, as we know, pursuant to P215, was drafted on the 14th of November I think, which means after this meeting. So it's unclear to me whether at the 8th of November meeting somebody was informed about something which followed subsequently, which was done later on. And in this sense I believe that some confusion may be engendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, Defence counsel examined the witness in respect of P317, which is the aide-memoire for this co-ordination meeting, at which time he asked him whether or not the implementation of the war plan had been finished. Now, the implementation of the war plan was the implementation of a directive by President Milosevic to create a war plan. This witness testified that they had done so up to a certain level, but below certain echelons they had not because he did not believe that it was going to be -- essentially, he thought it was a futile exercise. And therefore, he did not have his lower echelons implement the plan. What I have asked this witness is: Did you inform the people who attended the meeting on the 8th of November, when President Milosevic suggested or said that a war plan should be created, that he didn't follow through? That's the question I've asked him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah, you're not addressing the issue of dates that Mr. Lukic is raising. And -- and -- You see, with all these documents not before us at the same time, it is very difficult for me also to follow. I can't just -- I'm not with you just looking at one document. I would like to see all of them before me and the various dates of each document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm just reading, for a moment, Mr. Lukic's intervention.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may be of assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, from what I understand Mr. Lukic's intervention to be, is that -- let me outline the dates, Your Honour. The first date that's relevant is the 8th of November; that is the Mladic diary entry where President Milosevic says: Prepare a war plan. That's the 8th of November. Now, this document that we have before us is December of 1993. Mr. Lukic took --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, just a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, you said the document before us. What is it called?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This document is called an aide-memoire for the co-ordination of tasks at the VJ on 17 December 1993, so this is a document -- and the document itself, then, if we turn to page 3, is dated the 17th of December.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: All right. And --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay? So what Mr. Lukic -- I understood the examination of Mr. Lukic when he took the witness to the passage I have referred to, he asked him whether the plan, the war plans, had been fully developed and had been achieved up to the corps level. That's the war plan that Milosevic had suggested be prepared on the 8th of November. And the plan in the -- and let me just follow additionally. Following that meeting, in fact, at the end of the diary entry D442, there are entries from General Mladic outlining who on behalf of the VRS was to prepare that directive and that plan. And we have evidence in the record that General Mladic, in fact, followed through. And there are -- the complete VRS Drina War Plan is in the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, D442 -- you said D442.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That is the diary entry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And what is the date of that entry?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: 8 of November.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. But the 8 of November, that's when you say Slobodan Milosevic said, Prepare a war plan?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Fine. And is it on the same day that Mladic also follows up with --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And then in that same -- in 442 MFI, you see at the end of that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah, and I'm saying --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: -- entry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- what is the date of the entry in 442?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, the date of the entry that I'm referring to is the 8th of November, 19 -- that's the -- that's the -- if we can pull it up, I can -- if we can pull up D442.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for His Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I see Mr. Lukic is on his feet. You know, in my tradition, two counsel don't stand up at the same time. When the one is standing and the other one stands up, the one standing sits down. So I never know who to go to. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to help and speed things up and resolve this confusion in the most elegant way. If the question of Mr. Harmon is whether in the period since the creation of the Drina Plan, which was the 14th of November, 1993, until this co-ordination meeting, which is on the 17th of December, 1993, whether Mr. Novakovic -- the fact that that plan was not elaborated further than the Main Staff informed of that -- the participants of the 8th of November meeting, if that was his intention, I fully accept that kind of question, and I believe that the witness will be able to answer it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Can I --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- come up with a solution. Let's take a break, and you sort it out. You'll tell us when we come back. Court adjourned. Come back at quarter to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Has the issue been resolved, Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the question in English was -- what Mr. Novak Lukic says was correct and proper. The problem existed in the interpretation that he received and that was the source of the confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So just to, kind of, recap where we are, I have -- on the monitor, I have D442 MFI and I have the first page. And this is the meeting of the 8th of November, 1993, and it is the meeting where Milosevic says that a war plan had to be created. It identifies the participants in that meeting, including General Novakovic. And the question that I asked General Novakovic related to his testimony where he said: "At the corps level and lower, we did not draft the war plan."

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And my question, General Novakovic, was: Did you inform the participants who were identified, any of those participants, that you had not followed through and drafted the war plan at the lower-echelon levels?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, the war plan of the SVK was -- had been drafted earlier than that and had existed as such. However, my statement was this: The updating of the war plan in the spirit of the adopted joint war plan was not done deeper than the Main Staff and corps levels, which means the planning of the use of corps by the Main Staff in the spirit of what were the new elements of the joint war plan labelled "Drina."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, did you tell the participants of this meeting of the 8th of November, 1993, that you did not prepare the war plan at the corps level and lower? You can say yes; you can say no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Sir, the joint war plan or the Drina Plan was really quite important for the SVK in its survival, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Why was it important, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because pursuant to its provisions, if it were to be implemented, then the VJ and the VRS in a way would be participating in the defence of the RSK.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And if the VJ and the VRS were to be participating in the defence of the RSK, it was important that the lower echelon units, the brigades and other units, have a plan of their own so they knew how to discharge their responsibilities under the plan; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In fact, the lower echelons were instructed to draft a war plan, Drina, that applied to their own echelon levels, and I'm talking below the corps level. That was, in fact, the case; they were given an order to do so, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In accordance with the new war plan, Mr. Harmon, their missions and tasks remained the same because the next step that was necessary for the level below the corps level, meaning brigades and lower, to elaborate the new elements of the plan of use of the SVK was missing, did not materialise.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could we have XN100 on the monitor. And I would like B/C/S page 56 to be displayed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: XN, is that a new document?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is for impeachment purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may first see the document on the screen before I voice my opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You need to see it -- do you have a copy? Okay. Let's wait for the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you. If it's used only for the purposes of impeachment, then I stipulate. I agree that this document be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Sir, this is a document - take a look at it - it is dated the 17th of March, 1995, and it's entitled: "Destruction of the invalidated PU." Now, what does "PU" stand for, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Plan of Use" or "Engagement Plan."

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. And do you see -- at the bottom, do you see a signature?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Commander Lieutenant-Colonel Rade Medic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you know him?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: He was the commander of the 1st Light Infantry -- or light brigade of the SVK. Sir, this is an order, as you can see, and it says: "Pursuant to the 7th Corps command order ..." it gives a number, "regarding the drafting and coming into force of the new engagement plan, I hereby order: "1. By means of a commission, execute the destruction of the 1st Light Brigade 'Drina' Engagement Plan valid to date, as well as excerpts from the 7th Corps Engagement Plan, invalidated through the drafting of a new PU." Then sub-part 2: "I hereby designate the following persons in the commission for the destruction of documents from the 'Drina' Engagement Plan ..." So it's clear, is it not, General Novakovic, that a -- the 1st Light Brigade had a plan, a Drina Engagement Plan, for their own use; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, did they draft the 1st Light Brigade Drina Engagement Plan on their own initiative?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: They would have had to -- they would have drafted the 1st Light Brigade Drina Engagement Plan pursuant to an order from a higher authority; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, when the joint war plan Drina was drafted, we created the new plan at the level of the Main Staff down to the level of corps. But as far as brigades are concerned, concerning the 1st Light Brigade, it be included, what they had before that in terms of missions and tasks, pursuant to the erstwhile plan of use, without any new elements from the Drina War Plan, they just copied, pasted it, and labelled it the Drina War Plan. This is what I'm trying to tell you. And this -- I mean, by the fact that there were no reshuffling of areas of responsibility or issuance of any new tasks and missions to units at brigade and lower levels, which would then have meant a drafting of a new war plan and determining, within the Drina Plan of new missions, new areas of responsibility, et cetera. And this may be the reason for the confusion about the reasons why this did not happen. This is just labelling and titling. The plans of use of all brigades remained the same. And this is what I'm claiming.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Sir, you earlier testified that there was a war plan for the SVK. You said when there was -- the Drina Plan was a joint war plan. It involved integrating the forces of the VRS and the VJ into the SVK war plan. So this was -- the war plan that was in the possession of the 1st Light Brigade did not have the use of the VJ and the use of the VRS in it. Those were new elements that had to be incorporated into the creation of the Drina Plan; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, new elements from the joint war plan, Drina, which should have been incorporated into the planning of the use of units at the brigade level, implied providing detailed instructions as to where, into what zone each of the units would arrive from the Army of Yugoslavia and the Army of Republika Srpska, either as part of the first echelon of the Army of the Republika Srpska Krajina or the second echelon. I here claim that the plan was not further elaborated, either the level of the Army of Yugoslavia, as far as I know, as well as the Army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. The commanders of those units which should have been deployed as per the Drina War Plan, the first necessary step in order to provide a very precise mission to those units and the units of our army, of the Army of Republika Srpska -- Serbian Krajina, that step was never taken by the Army of Yugoslavia. And that is why now you have a new plan labelled "Drina." But the missions and tasks are only of the units of the VJ but were not elaborated at the lower level of the VJ. The further step of the elaboration was never carried out, either at the level of the VJ or the level of the Army of Republika Srpska Krajina. It was never done. It was never carried out. If that had been done, then we would now be in a position to say that a new war plan, the new war plan, Drina, was elaborated at all levels. The Main Staff of the Army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina could not do it on its own.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Well, you told us that the Army of the Republika Srpska Krajina couldn't do it on its own, that's why the Drina Plan was, in fact, created. So you could have a plan that integrated the use of forces of the VRS and the VJ in conjunction with the SVK. That was what the Drina Plan was, a joint war plan; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, I don't know whether you said it, but it was interpreted to me that you are asking me about the Army of Republika Srpska, whereas I can't say anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me repeat my question because it's apparent you did not understand my question. The Drina War Plan was a joint war plan describing the use of three -- of the VRS, the VJ, and the SVK. That was the Drina War Plan; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We have a document in front of us that is from the command of the 1st Light Brigade, and my question is: Who, to your knowledge, ordered them to prepare a Drina Plan that related to the 1st Light Brigade? You said in your earlier evidence: "We did not draft a war plan at the corps levels or lower." The command of the 1st Light Brigade apparently had drafted a Drina Engagement Plan that related to the use of their forces. How did it come about that they drafted a Drina Engagement Plan that related to the 1st Light Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why we keep on talking at cross-purposes. The 1st Light Brigade did not draft the Drina War Plan. They just used their former plan of use that they previously had. They marked it as "Drina" because as of then the entire plan of the use of VRSK was labelled Drina. And as of then, that document was used in the 1st Light Brigade, and all the other brigades of the 7th Corps was called Drina. However, it contained the same elements as the previous war plan. And that was not done for the reasons that I already mentioned in my previous evidence. If you need me to do so, I will repeat all of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, who ordered the 1st Light Brigade to mark their plan "Drina Plan"? You say they just marked it "Drina Plan," but there was no plan -- who ordered them to mark it "Drina Plan"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It could only have been ordered by the command of the 7th Corps, which was their superior command. And as for the command of 7th Corps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just -- you've answered my question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, let me direct your attention, on this document, General Novakovic, to the passage above the word "order." If you could focus your attention on that. It says: "Pursuant to the 7th Corps command ..." and then it gives numbers, "regarding the drafting and coming into force of the new Engagement Plan." Do you know what the new engagement plan was called?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 17 March 1995 is the date. Subsequently, I heard that the name of that war plan was Gvozd, G-v-o-z-d, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We'll turn to a different topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could I have that last exhibit, Your Honour, entered into evidence, given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is so entered. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, I'm advised that this exhibit consists of 90 pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It is the B/C/S page 56. And let me just check on the English page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the English page would be ET 0672-6894.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May we please then give that page -- those pages an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, the pages indicated will be Exhibit P2921.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: General Novakovic, are you familiar with the Orkan rocket system?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you describe what that system is?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a rocket system which was used for support in the JNA, as far as I remember, and it was used on one occasion.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: It was manufactured for the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. And you say it was used on one occasion. On which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that the witness said that it was manufactured for the JNA as just one piece of equipment. It was a once-only exercise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure. But, you see, even that answer does not answer the question put to you. The question put to you was: Can you describe what that system is. Not for whom it was manufactured and how many times. Can you explain what it is and how it operates? If you can't, "I cannot explain." If you can, you can tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What does "no" mean? Do you mean, no, you cannot explain? You are not able to explain? My question didn't call for a "no" answer; it called for -- oh, yeah, you cannot explain. Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me see if you can affirm what I will be telling you in just a minute, sir. The Orkan rocket system was -- its primary military use was to target soldiers and armoured vehicles; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't confirm that. I can't say anything about the armoured vehicles because as far as I know armoured vehicles were not targeted by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm talking about its use in warfare. Its use in warfare was to target soldiers and armoured vehicles. Do you agree with that proposition or disagree with that proposition?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly switch off all unnecessary mikes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All rocket systems, including Orkan, are used to destroy targets in the process of attack against manpower attacking in open spaces or groups of enemy soldiers which are based somewhere stationary or on the move.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And the Orkan rocket system was fitted with either a warhead containing bomblets or anti-tank shells; is that correct, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that that's correct. I believe that it had a warhead and in the warhead it also had cluster bombs. And when it comes to using Orkan against armoured vehicles or tanks, I don't know whether it was ever used against armoured vehicles or tanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Would the Orkan rocket system be a suitable system to fire in populated areas?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, it is intended for targeting targets in the space in a certain area, in the area where enemy soldiers are deployed, especially when those soldiers are in the process of attacking or while they are in their bases. As for settled areas, only if such a military base is separate from that settled area, if it is clearly separated from the settled area, or if there is a clear warning and repeated warning to the civilian population that they should move away from a military target and seek shelter in a secure area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, can you -- are you familiar with the LUNA rocket system, and can you describe what it is and its use?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a rocket system with a range of around 65 kilometres which is used to target significant targets of -- needless to say military targets within that range of the enemy territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you know what its accuracy is?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that its deviation is around 1 kilometre or up to 1 kilometre, which is a maximum if you do not have a full set of data available to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Would a LUNA rocket be a suitable weapons system to employ against a populated area?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, there's no single system which should be used in a populated area. All combat systems are intended to open fire against military targets. When there is a civilian population in such zones and the civilian populations was not previously alerted that such weapons would be used, then I suppose that any use of such weaponry systems would be inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In your evidence in chief, you were critical of the Orkan rocket attacks on Zagreb that occurred on the 2nd and 3rd of May, 1995; can you explain why?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stated that in the statement that I previously provided. I said also that it was a morally and politically unacceptable action because there was non-selective fire opened on a populated area. And I also stated in the statement that you must have, I'm sure, that the only thing that resulted from that was damages to one's own people that were then exposed to even more repercussions in a situation when it was already in the hands of the Croatian army. And I also said that there was no justification for such an act.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: While you were commander of the SVK, how many Orkan rocket systems were at your disposal?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One rocket system, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was special authorisation required to use the Orkan rocket system?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So any artillery commander could fire Orkan rockets at any time he wished?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand a link between the existence of a base and the authority of an artillery commander. That's the interpretation that I've received, but I can't establish a link between the two terms, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Let me try again. You had one Orkan rocket system. Whose authority was required to be given before it could be used?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two cases were required to issue such a permission: The first case was an order by the Main Staff, when that system was under the command of the Main Staff, which it was. And the second case was when the rocket system was assigned to a corps command which requested it in view of the shape of the territory. And the range of that system, it had to be moved from one corps zone to another when necessary. And in that case, it would have been the corps commander who would have issued an order for its use.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And the corps commander did not need the approval of the Main Staff to fire Orkan rockets?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it was resubordinated to him, in such a situation the answer would be no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. And was the Orkan rocket system resubordinated to corps commanders while you were the commander of the SVK?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In certain situations, the Orkan system was resubordinated to various corps commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What were those situations?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When an all-out Croatian offensive was launched in January 1993 in the area of Maslenica, Ravni Kotari, Velebit Mountain, and the Cetina River valley, there came a time when the Orkan system was resubordinated to the commander of the 7th Corps. This is what I remember very well. There may have been other such cases, but as I sit here I can't remember, so I can't testify to that with any certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. In respect of the LUNA rocket system, I ask you the same questions. First of all: How many LUNA rocket systems did you have in the SVK while you were the commander?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to the rocket -- to the Orkan rocket system, or ... ?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No, sir, I asked you about the LUNA rocket system.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: None, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Are you saying that while you were the commander of the SVK, the SVK did not have any LUNA rockets?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I'm saying is that we did not have any LUNA rocket system in the SVK.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, did you ever advocate, General Novakovic, that rockets be fired against Zagreb if towns in the RSK were attacked?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Rockets fired at Zagreb? Only at military targets, Mr. Harmon. And I believe that all that should be put in a context and explained as part of the context.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, let's take a look at 65 ter 6171.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is that a new document?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What is the --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It is for impeachment purposes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. You may proceed, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm waiting for the English version to come on the monitor, Your Honour. I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Sir, this is a document --

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: -- that is dated the 9th of June, 1993. It is from the Republika Serbia Krajina Main Staff of the Serbian army. And it is addressed to Slobodan Milosevic, the president of the Republic of Serbia. And can we turn to the last page of the document. You see two signatures at the bottom of this document, General Novakovic. Can you --

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: -- identify those signatures, please.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the left is my signature and on the right is Mr. Martic's signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could we turn to the second page in English and the second page in the Serbian language.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay, sir, this --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm directing Your Honours' attention and General Novakovic's attention to the passage in the English version that starts at the third paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And for your benefit, General Novakovic, it reads -- the passage I'm referring to is: "The Croatian Army is numerically and technically superior. The beginning of an all-out aggression is expected on 11 June 1993, even though 10 or 18 June 1993 are also being mentioned as critical dates. "So far we have undertaken the following measures:" And then if you go down to the portion that is underscored, it says: "We moved P-65 LUNA rockets from the Army Republika Srpska to the area of Banija and Kordun to prevent aggression or carry out possible attacks on Zagreb, should our towns come under attack." You see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that absolutely clearly, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, in your letter to President Milosevic, you express clearly that should there be an attack on the area, that you would carry out possible attacks on Zagreb should your towns come under attack. There is no reference in this document to military targets, is there?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, kindly -- at least let's not ignore what is stated in here. Would you allow me to read everything? If this is something to impeach me, let's read what it says here. Please. I'm --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you show me where it refers to military targets in this document?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot show you anywhere, but I can show you where it reads "as means of a deterrent" and "possible action" and point out the fact that I'm a co-author of this document, not the sole author, Mr. Prosecutor, but co-author.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's fine. We can see that from the document, that you are a co-author of this document, and you obviously read the document before you signed it.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously. I do claim that I signed it as a co-author of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And you asked me whether in our composition we had LUNA R-65 rockets. No, we did not have them, and this is clearly seen here from this document. A battalion of LUNA was part of the VRS, and the document clearly states that that battalion was rebased from the Army of Republika Srpska. I don't know how can you impeach me in terms of my statement that the SVK did not have in possession any LUNA rockets.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could we turn to XN310, please, and this is -- I'm sorry, could this document be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P2922.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And I suppose --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, this is -- this next document is for purposes of impeachment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not have any objections for that document to be used for those purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Sir, this is an order. It's dated the 28th of August, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
