utterances.text: Could we go to the last page in the -- actually, the second page in the English and I think the last page in the Serbian-language version.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You see a typed name at the end of this order, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No verbal response]

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Sir, do you see a typed name at the end of the order?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harmon. And I do not challenge this. This is not contentious.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could we turn to the next page in the English version, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: At the bottom -- not the stamp but at the bottom of the order it indicates to whom -- to which units the order was delivered. It starts with the 7th and the 15th and the 21st, 39th, 18th, and 11th, and then, in brackets, the 75th Logistics Base and the 105th, and it says "VBR." Are those the units to which this order was delivered?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, these are corps commands, logistics base, and the air brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The air brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell us what the acronym "VBR" stands for?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which acronym do you mean, Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: At the end of the list of addressees, it says "VBR."

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned a minute ago, the 105 Air Brigade, Air Force Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could we go to the first page in the English and the first page in the Serbian-language version.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, under the word "order, I hereby order the following," I'd like to direct your attention on paragraph 1. It reads: "Plan activities against military targets in Sibenik, Sinj, Zadar, Gospic, Ogulin, Karlovac, Sisak, Sunja, Osijek, and Vinkovci." And then it says: "In case of artillery attacks against Knin, plan targeting Zagreb as well." Now, this doesn't say anything about military targets in Zagreb, does it?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In item 1, which determines the sense of everything stated here, in the area following the word "I order," Mr. Harmon, it is clearly stated "against military targets." If civilian targets were meant, then they would have been listed and expressly stated. What this text discusses are military targets, action against which is being planned with artillery weapons which have deviations from metres to couple of tens of metres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, we do not have much time, and I'm sure you'd like to go home. You've been here for a very long time. It would be very helpful if you could please listen carefully to the question and answer the question only. Don't divert to other things. The question to you is simply this, that where Zagreb is mentioned, there is no mention of targeting military targets in Zagreb. Can you see the third line of that paragraph? Not the first line. Now you're referring us to the first line when the question is about the third line.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: "In case of artillery attacks against Knin, plan targeting Zagreb as well." Not: "Military targets in Zagreb." That's the question that is put to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Harmon, it is correct that not only for Zagreb but also for no of the towns and areas listed here where action by artillery is planned for, it doesn't state what types of targets is enumerated because that is made reference to in the first line of that paragraph. I don't know why we're singling out Zagreb here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We're singling out Zagreb, Mr. Novakovic, because for Sibenik, Sinj, Zadar, Gospic, Ogulin, Karlovac, Sisak, Sunja, Osijek, and Vinkovci, you say they must target military targets; but you don't say they must target military targets when you come to Zagreb. That's the distinction. And the question that is being put to you is: Why do you have not -- why have you not targeted military targets with respect to Zagreb? It's a very simple question. I don't know what the problem is. Yes, Mr. Lukic, you ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to point out a discrepancy in the English translation of this sentence with the original because in the original after the word "Vinkovci" there is a comma. And "in the case of artillery attacks against Knin, plan targeting Zagreb." In the English version, those are two separate sentences.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I stick by my explanation. It is stated above: "Military targets." And everything that is referred to below that means military targets in all those areas, including Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Novakovic. Yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In that same first entry, sir, let me direct your attention to the following passage. It says: "The commanders of the 39th Corps and the 21st Corps should be ready for targeting Zagreb with R-65, surface -- R-65, as well as for reception of Orkan multiple rocket-launchers." Now, the R-65 system is the LUNA rocket system, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harmon. And these are areas from which it was possible to target military targets in the area of Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And whose R-65 LUNA rockets were to be deployed by the 39th Corps and the 21st Corps on the 28th of August, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned already once that those were the rocket systems from the VRS, Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And how many -- how long did you essentially have on loan the R-65 LUNA rocket system? Let me repeat the question because you look confused, sir. How long did you have on loan from the VRS the R-65 LUNA rocket systems? Did you have them for a month? Did you have them for a week? Did you have them for a year? Did you have them for the entire time you were the commander of the SVK?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In events when our estimates were that threat is increased on the basis of intelligence available to us, we requested that certain weaponry or a battalion of such rockets were brought to the territory of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. Such periods could have lasted for ten days, 15 days. I don't believe that there ever was a full month.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So it's fair to say, isn't it, while you assert that the SVK did not have any LUNA rocket systems of their own, they had at their disposal LUNA rocket systems from the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The procedure was as follows: When our estimate was that --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Sir, can you just answer my question. My question was this - I'm not interested in the procedure. You assert that there were no LUNA rocket systems in the SVK that you owned. My question was: You had them at their -- at your disposal from the VRS; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Harmon. We had them at our disposal temporarily from time to time, whenever they responded positively to our requests.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. That's the answer. Thank you very much, sir. Now, let me -- in September of 1993, did you launch rocket attacks against Jastrebarsko and other cities?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you use Orkan rockets against those targets in September of 1993?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, Orkan rockets were used against some of the targets there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you use Orkan rockets against Samobor in September of 1993?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Harmon. Those rockets were used to target barracks housing the communications unit of the Main Staff of the Croatian army. As far as I can remember, Orkan rockets were used against that target.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And were those -- was that target in the town of Samobor?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That target was next to the town of Samobor, and the population had been publicly warned about those -- that target being targeted for several days prior to the attack over our public media.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you tell us, if you can recall, how many Orkan rockets were fired against the town of Samobor?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: None at the town of Samobor, Mr. Harmon, but at the base of the communications for the Main Staff of the Croatian army. And I can't recall how many missiles were used.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. In November of 1993, did you fire Orkan rockets and LUNA rockets at Jastrebarsko and Samobor again?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In November 1993, if I understood your question correctly?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall that, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could we look at XN403, please. Your Honour, I've been reminded to please request XN310 be given a number -- an exhibit number, if it could be given one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2923, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And XN403, for what purpose?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Impeachment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could I have page 1 of the English, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Sir, this is a newspaper article from "Vjesnik" dated the 13th of November, 1993. Where is the newspaper "Vjesnik" located, in which country?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Zagreb, in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. And this article is entitled: "Serbian War Criminals are Stepping Up Their Attacks Against Croatian Towns." And then it says: "'Orkan' and 'LUNA' missiles fired from territory under UN protection." And I want to direct your attention, sir, to B/C/S, the first page, in particular, sir, in the left-hand column, the first two paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, it is under the location Zagreb and then the first two paragraphs I direct Your Honours' attention to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And what this article reports, General Novakovic, is that, in the first paragraph: "... around 8.00 a.m., four 'Orkan' rocket missiles hit the Samobor region. No one was killed, but three persons were wounded." And then it says, in the next paragraph: "Three 'Orkan' missiles fell ... simultaneously on the area of Jastrebarsko. Several persons were injured and several houses were damaged. A state of emergency was declared for the area of Jastrebarsko. Explosives experts removed the scattered 'bomblets,' and the citizens have been warned not to touch these objects." Does this newspaper article, sir, refresh your recollection as to whether Orkan rockets were fired in the Samobor region and at Jastrebarsko in November of 1993?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to scroll up the B/C/S document because of the date. I don't want to suggest anything. Mr. Harmon is asking questions with reference to November. Could the witness state which date the newspaper bears?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This I did not write. This is not what I invented. This would be Zagreb, Monday, 30th -- 13th of September, 1993. This is the date on the front page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that correction. The English translation I have is an error, Your Honour. I've been operating off the English translation since I do not read Cyrillic. And let me ask you, sir, having been -- seeing the correct date of September, does this refresh your recollection as to whether Orkan rockets were fired at those two locations?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, Orkan rockets were not used in action against those two towns. They were used against the bases of the Croatian army, as I've already stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And where were those bases? Tell me where the bases of those armies were located, General Novakovic.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You asked me about Samobor. Quite next to Samobor there was a barracks, and I know for sure that it is located outside the settled area. The barracks near Jastrebarsko is located north of the town of Jastrebarsko. Sisak was on the very front line, Mr. Harmon. In Sisak, Croatian forces were located there and our forces were located on the outskirts, in the suburbs of Sisak. Just as it was the case in Gospic, Kutina, Ivanic-Grad -- well, Kutina and Ivanic-Grad were maybe 10 to 15 kilometres from the front line. And Gospic was next to the front line. Pirovac -- well, I think it's in Dalmatia; I don't know where it is. This was done around the time of the Medak Pocket, while the Croatian forces massacred the civilian population in the Medak Pocket, where we repeated for days what civilian targets we are going to target over the media. I would like you to trust me, Mr. Harmon. You don't have to. Most of the targets that we threatened to target were in Zagreb, but none of those missiles from no weapons systems were fired against Zagreb. This was a certain dose of threat with previous announcement being made to the civilians. And I repeat: No missiles were fired at Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can we turn, in this same exhibit, then, to B/C/S page 2 and English page 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We will have to mark it for identification pending the correction of the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour -- no, I'm -- Your Honour, I'm asking if we could just turn to a different page. I'm not asking for its admission yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Oh, I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The English page is page 3 and the B/C/S page is page 2. Or if -- the English page would be ET 0424-9858.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And, sir, I'm directing your attention to the column on the left of this document. It looks like it's fairly small.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: To -- no, below that, please. Could you go a little bit lower than that, please. Yes, Thank you. Keep going, scrolling down. That's fine. Thank you. And, Your Honours, I'm directing Your Honours' attention to the first para -- the first portion under "Galbraith in Karlovac and Lucko."

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And, sir, this article refers to a visit to the -- in the Zagreb -- I'm sorry, in the Lucko settlement near Zagreb where ambassador -- US Ambassador to Croatia Peter Galbraith visited. And I'm going to quote this. And he says -- and he spoke with the local population: "As a consequence of these attacks, many houses have been destroyed and 12 people have been wounded. The American ambassador noted" -- noted, "... he described the 'rocket attack on Zagreb' as an 'obvious act of terror.' No military goals can be accomplished by launching attacks on areas inhabited by civilians. The ambassador expressed his sympathy with the victims of both attacks." Your comments, please.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot comment, Mr. Harmon, because this is a newspaper article from a newspaper in war which engaged in war propaganda against the other side. How many people suffered injuries? Well, what I only can say is that I received information from UNPROFOR officers that the rockets aimed at barracks of special police in the Lucko Garrison, which is located at the airport - and airport, of course, presumes that there are no major settlements around it - that there were no casualties or victims there; that a crater was created when -- where the missile impacted and exploded. What the propaganda was derived from that, that's another question in terms of what the journalists wrote. You can read plenty other things if you were to scroll up.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I note the time. And I will seek the admission of this document after we take a break, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We'll take a break and come back at half past 12.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, two matters: The first matter is I would move for admission of XN403, ask that it be given an exhibit number. Because I need to then address the next exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And it will be marked for identification pending the correction of the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be MFI P2924.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the reason I asked the witness to step out because I think we're going to have a brief discussion on the next exhibit which I would like to introduce for both -- possibly impeachment but also for the truth of the matter. It is XN343. I can explain what it is, Your Honour. It is a Croatian judgement against General Novakovic. It's a judgement where he was convicted in absentia for war crime against the civilian population, the use of prohibited combat equipment, and destroying cultural and historical monuments. He was sentenced to 20 years' imprisonment. I'm not seeking to introduce the document for the truth of the contents of it, only for the truth that there is a judgement against him for the three crimes that I have described and that he has been sentenced to a term of imprisonment of 20 years. There is a description in here that found him guilty of certain specific attacks. I intend to put to the witness those elements, but I'm not introducing the document for the truth of those matters, if I make myself clear. It's a fairly long judgement. It describes specific incidents. I'm not introducing this document -- attempting to introduce this document for that. I can tell you, Your Honour, about the background of this document, when we received it, and the like. We disclosed it to the Defence on the 23rd of June, 2010, by CD. We received it on the 25th of July, 2001. We had no reason to disclose it earlier because General Novakovic was not on our witness list, he was only on the Defence witness list. And therefore we only disclosed it on the 23rd of June, 2010, when we -- it was confirmed that he would in fact, you know, be coming to testify before this Tribunal. I think it is in the interest of justice that the Court be aware there is a judgement against General Novakovic in Zagreb as a result of a trial in absentia and the nature of those charges. Those are my submissions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am against the introduction of this decision into evidence. In this judgement, the reference is made to some things which are beyond the description of what is the -- part of the jurisprudence of this Tribunal. Certain crimes are described, or rather, facts in connection with those crimes, and the judgement was passed in absentia. It is true that we were disclosed by the -- this document by the Prosecution. I believe that this is an attempt on the part of Mr. Harmon to introduce something through the backdoor which has to do something with the indictment because Mile Novakovic is one of the persons listed in the indictment against General Perisic, and within that context the Prosecution should have expressed interest in a document of this nature even earlier and not only when it found -- was found on the list of the Defence witnesses. I don't object to Mr. Harmon asking the witness whether he knows that he had been tried and sentenced in Croatia in absentia and what was the case against him, but I object to the document being introduced because it goes beyond the purpose of impeaching the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Any reply?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have no reply, Your Honour. I made my submissions and I stand by them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You see, Mr. Harmon, in your first submissions you made two contradictory statements, and I would like to get clarity. You first started by saying you are introducing the document for both impeachment and possibly -- also for the truth of it. And later you said not for the truth of it but just for the -- to prove that there's a judgement that exists. Now, I'm not quite sure what your purpose is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I obviously did not make myself very clear. I apologise, Your Honour. I don't know if this witness is going to admit that he has been convicted in Croatia for certain crimes or not. So in terms of impeachment, I'm somewhat waiting to hear his answer on that. So I may be introducing it for purposes of impeachment. Nevertheless, I am seeking its admission for the truth that there exists in Croatia a judgement against him for three crimes and a sentence of 20 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: (redacted) so I anticipate that he may or may not know of the existence of this. It might be my belief that he probably does. But -- so that's the first issue. The second issue, Your Honour, is, there is described in this judgement lots of facts about an incident on such and such a day, such and such happened on this day, it describes what happened, and it also describes - I'm interested in particular - in this document on the charges dealing with the Orkan rocket attacks. I'm not interested in the incidents that deal with the artillery attacks on certain locations on certain dates. I'm not seeking its admission --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, my attention has been brought to a fact that previously when we discussed these kind of things we were in private session. Do the parties want to go into private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If that's what the practice has been. I'm not aware of that practice, Your Honour, in terms of ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Fine. Then I apologise, Your Honour. That's not my intention to divulge such a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My problem, Mr. Harmon, is you keep saying you want to introduce it to prove that there is a judgement against the accused -- against the witness, and then you also want to refer to the facts. You see, if it is just to prove that there is a judgement against him, then you are a little premature. You can always rise with it if he denies the existence of a judgement, number one. Number two: If it does go in for that purpose and that purpose only, then we don't even need to read it, we don't even need to know what is in there. Those are findings of a court; it's not evidence. And we just say, There is this document which says you have been convicted and you have been sentenced to 20 years for certain crimes. That's all. Now, I can understand the concern that has been raised by Mr. Lukic because if you -- if it comes in and it is -- we are expected to read it, then we are going to get a whole lot of other things that you do not purport to prove.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am not interested in polluting the record, taking advantage of a document that has facts that are not -- I'm not asserting here. I'm going to ask the witness about the facts in the attacks for which he has been convicted; that's my intention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I will get his answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Right. And if he admits them, there's no need for you to tender the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That is true. I suspect he won't admit it. I'm just anticipating. But we may be able to resolve this in a slightly different way. I mean, it may well be that Mr. Lukic and I can prepare a stipulation that could be accepted by the Court; the stipulation being that there is a judgement of conviction against General Novakovic and it was as a result of a trial in absentia and he was convicted of the crimes that I described and he was sentenced to 20 years. I'm perfectly satisfied to do that -- have that solution adopted as well. But that depends on Mr. Lukic and whether he's willing to enter into such a stipulation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot say yes to that for a simple reason. This judgement was passed in absentia. And you know what the standards are of a trial in absentia and what is the essence of facts adjudicated in that way. I would have to discuss it with Mr. Harmon and see what the wording of that stipulation would be. I can accept that there is a judgement passed in the Republic of Croatia by which certain persons were convicted in absentia, among them is Mr. Novakovic, who was sentenced to a term of 20 years, if that is enough at the moment by way of answering Mr. Harmon's proposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think what we should then do is call the witness in and you put the questions to him. And if he denies, then you can sort out what the content of the stipulation shall be.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's satisfactory. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. May the witness please come in.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Just for the record, Your Honour, are we in open session? I just want to confirm that we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's what I thought. Okay. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: General Novakovic, are you aware that you were convicted in Croatia for a war crime committed against the civilian population for the use of prohibited combat equipment and for destroying cultural and historical monuments and that that trial was in absentia?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do have information of that kind, although I'm not aware of any details.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And when you say you're not aware of any details, are you aware of the fact that the conviction, the judgement against you in Croatia is for committing a war crime against the civilian population for the use of prohibited combat equipment and for destroying cultural and historical monuments?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard of a conviction of that kind. Mr. Harmon, in the war I heard of at least three such convictions, so I really don't know what exactly are you referring to at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What I'm referring to at this moment is the existence of a judgement in Croatia against you for those -- for having committed those three crimes.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up to February 1993, Mr. Harmon, Croatian media published at least three times, usually on the eve of some negotiations, that I had been sentenced to a 20-year term in prison as a Serbian terrorist, and it happened at least three times.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. Now, did you, sir, on the 28th of February, 1993, attack the Croatian towns of Vodice and Zaton with Orkan rockets?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before the witness answers, could you, Your Honours, warn him about the rights not to incriminate himself by answering this question and similar ones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, you have the right not to answer questions that will incriminate you in any proceedings that may or may be instituted against you. And I know that you came here as a witness, you don't have a lawyer with you, but you are also entitled, should you need legal assistance in how to deal with these questions, you are entitled to consult one and get advice from him or her on how to deal with the questions. Would you like to have a lawyer to assist you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is no reason for that, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. If you don't need a lawyer, just be aware, then, that you have been warned. And when you answer any questions, you have the right not to incriminate yourself. And we hope that you will be able to identify the questions that you think might incriminate you and where you want to react differently. Okay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me just remind you what Mr. Harmon told you a little earlier this morning. When you nod your head, it doesn't get typed in. So we -- that's why I look at you. Even when you nod your head, we still want you to say something so that the stenographer can type it for us. Okay? Yes, Mr. Lukic -- Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me repeat my question, General Novakovic. Did you or your forces, on the 28th of February, 1993, attack the Croatian towns of Vodice and Zaton with Orkan rockets?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, I didn't order any such thing. That's the truth. Whether such attacks happened or not, I'm not in a position to know because I never dealt with an issue of that particular date and who did what on that particular date, who attacked whom.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did your forces attack Sibenik on the 2nd of March, 1993, with Orkan rockets?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, I can't confirm that for any of those dates. When you put it to me like that, whatever I answered would be pure speculation on my part.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm going to put a series of questions and -- relating -- the same type of question with a series of dates and locations, and I just ask you to answer those questions. Sir, on the 11th of March, 1993, did your forces attack Sibenik with Orkan rockets?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. As I sit here, I can't answer your question, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: On the 22nd of March, 1993, did your forces attack Sibenik with Orkan rockets?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: On the 23rd of March, 1993, did your forces attack Sibenik with Orkan rockets?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the same reason, I can't answer any questions about any dates 17 or 18 years ago, and that includes this particular date as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have one more date for you, General Novakovic, it's the 14th of April, 1993, did your forces attack Sibenik with Orkan rockets?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that either, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you recall, while you were commander of the SVK, ever giving an order to your forces to attack Sibenik with Orkan rockets?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's -- the way I framed this isn't -- doesn't go for -- get me a precise answer. You don't recall doing it -- did you in fact, while you were commander of the SVK, order your forces to attack Sibenik with Orkan rockets?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't issue any such orders. If I had, I'm sure that I would have remembered.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you -- again, while you were the commander of the SVK, did you give any orders to your forces to attack Sibenik with LUNA rockets?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: LUNA rockets? Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Did you, while you were the commander of the SVK, give your forces any order, any orders whatsoever, to attack Sibenik?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps I issued an order to launch attacks against military targets in the general area of Sibenik. That is something I can't rule out.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What were the military targets in Sibenik while you were the commander of the SVK?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, the Sibenik harbour, the Zadar harbour, Sapurine were places where the Croatian army forces were brought in to be deployed in that area. They were brought in from the depth of Croatia and from Herzegovina. Our scouts observed that process. Moreover, in the general area of Sibenik, Biograd [Realtime translation read in error "Beograd"], and in that part there - and we're talking about settlements right behind the front line - there were artillery batteries there operated by the Croatian army. There were also command posts which could also make perfect military targets. And if such a military target was detected, he was attacked by the most appropriate artillery means.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Who is "he"? Mr. Novakovic, you are interpreted as having said: "... if such a military target was detected, he was attacked by the most appropriate artillery means."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter corrects herself: It was attacked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just to avoid confusion and for the record, page 67, line 6, there is a reference to Beograd, and I believe the witness actually wanted to refer to another city, just to avoid confusion and to make the record clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, when you said: "Our scouts observed that process. Moreover, in the general area of Sibenik ..." and which town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Biograd.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you happy, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: B-i.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: B-i?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: B-i-o-g-r-a-d? Okay. Biograd. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In January of 1993 in -- when the Croat offensive was launched in the area of Maslenica, Ravni Kotari, in the Velebit Mountain and in the Cetina River valley, did you use Orkan rockets as a response to that military offensive?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, the Orkan rockets that you insist upon and other means that were at our disposal were not used as a response or retaliation; they were used to target military targets, which means forces on the front line were targeted, forces being brought in were targeted, artillery positions were targeted. That is the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So I take it the answer to my question is -- actually, let me ask you. Is the -- what is the answer to my question? My question was: In January of 1993 when there was a Croatian offensive launched in the areas I identified, did you use Orkan rockets as a response to that military offensive?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Orkan rocket system was resubordinated to the command of the 7th Corps, and the command of the 7th Corps which defended that area probably used it to target targets that they detected and which they thought should be targeted with that weaponry. And that would be my answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were you ever informed of what targets they used the Orkan rocket system against?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether this was part and parcel of regular combat reports that corps commanders submitted to the Main Staff. I can't remember now. The reports did not contain information on what weaponry was used to -- against which targets. It was a summary report on what kind of activities and combat operations were conducted along which axes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In the RSK, while you were commander, was there the -- a manufacturing capacity to make Orkan rockets that were necessary for that Orkan rocket system?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the manufacturing capacity to manufacture any kinds of munitions, that's something we did not have.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What was your source of supply for the Orkan rockets?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Harmon, in fairness to the witness, he testified before the break that they had one Orkan rocket-launcher, which was a once-off manufactured by the JNA, if I remember his testimony well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I remember that as well, Your Honour. But my question really was: What was the source of the rockets that were used in that, we can say, borrowed system from the VRS?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: From the JNA -- the rocket -- I beg your pardon. Oh, I beg your pardon. I beg your pardon. I'm thinking of the -- yeah, you're talking about the Orkan rocket?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. The LUNA rockets came from the VRS. The rocket -- the Orkan rocket came from the JNA, and it was only one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Fine. Well, then -- okay --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: According to his earlier testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you for correcting me, Your Honour. You're absolutely right. I was confused.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Sir, for your one Orkan rocket launching system, what was your source of supply for those rockets?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, we had a certain number of those rockets. And since that weapon was manufactured in the town of Travnik in Bosnia and Herzegovina, which was not under Serb control at the time, some of those rockets were in Republika Srpska. And I believe that a number of such rockets were in the VJ. I cannot be specific in terms of what I remember, rather, about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Following the offensive in -- Croatian offensive in January 1993, your supply, supply of Orkan rockets that were available to you, had been exhausted, hadn't they?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the bulk of those munitions were -- was spent, but rockets for the Orkan rocket system were not spent in great quantities. They were used to target what the commanders deemed as the most important targets - for instance, a large unit being brought in and a dangerous artillery position - in the view of the commander of the day, and that was the commander of the 7th Corps. Do you allow me a question, Mr. Harmon, for you?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, let me -- I want to ask the questions, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me have XN309 on the monitor, please, and it's for purposes of impeachment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me just take a look before I speak. I do not object to this document being used for impeachment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Sir, please examine the document that's in front of you. This is a document that is from the Republic of Serbian Krajina, General Staff of the Serbian army, and it's a request for ammunition supply to the General Staff of the VJ. The date on your copy and on my original copy is illegible, but there is a reference point in the text which gives us some guidance as to when this request was made. It -- this document says that: "You are familiar with the fact that we are in possession of the artillery rocket system 'Orkan' which is used in the entire area of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. Given that the armed forces of the Republic of Croatia launched an attack against the territory of the Republic of Serbian Krajina on 22nd January, 1993, we were forced to bring this artillery rocket system into action. Such a system is invaluable -- of invaluable importance to us, and it helped in many ways to stable the situation at the front line. The 262-millimetre rockets 'Orkan' which we had in stock have been used up so that we only have a minimum number left at our disposal, which makes any further artillery fire on our part in view of the expected spreading of the fighting impossible. "Given that we are in such a situation, we turn to you with a request to deliver to us approximately 200 rockets with fuses." So do you recall this request to the VJ General Staff that you issued, General Novakovic?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall specifically, but I'm not saying that I did not send it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And, in fact, following the offensive operations of the Croatian army that were launched against you -- in fact, you didn't have many Orkan rockets left, and you had to turn to available sources in the VJ to replenish your depleted stocks; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not understand the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me repeat the question, General Novakovic. I said: Following the offensive operations that the Croatian army launched against you in January of 1993, you did not have many Orkan rockets left, and you had to turn to available sources, that is, the VJ, to replenish your depleted stocks of Orkan rockets; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I allow for it being possible the same way that we addressed the Main Staff of the VRS in order for us to create stockpiles, because at the time those offensive operations continued. We didn't want to fall below a certain minimum of stocks.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, assist me, General Novakovic. During the time you were commander of the SVK, you had -- you've testified you had one Orkan rocket system in the SVK. Following your departure as commander of the SVK until the end of the war, did you acquire any additional Orkan rocket systems, or did you only have one Orkan rocket system throughout the war? In other words -- actually, let me strike that question. Throughout the war -- strike that. After you were the commander of the SVK, General Novakovic, did the SVK acquire an Orkan rocket system, or did it continue to rely on the VRS to lend you such systems?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Orkan system was --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, General Novakovic, let me interrupt you. I made a mistake, okay, and I want to correct that. Between the time you ended your period as commander of the SVK until the end of the war, how many Orkan rocket systems were available to you, the SVK?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After no longer being commander of the SVK, none of such were available to me. And the SVK had available just one system, as before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Sorry. Thank you, General Novakovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could I have this document marked as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P2925.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: General, I want to turn our attention to Operation Pauk, which you testified about. You seem to be shaking your head, General. Is there a problem?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have a major problem, Mr. Harmon. You expressed a compromising fact: that I have been convicted in Croatia for very grave offences. What -- let the Court check whether this is discrediting against me or discrediting to somebody else. Let me lay out the facts. And I would like to ask the Presiding Judge to allow me to do the following because I see it very important, and it goes to the credibility of me as a witness and as a human being.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Novakovic. Be brief, please. Don't be too long.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as the judgement is concerned, Your Honours, on the 23rd of September, 2003, I found out about that judgement in the following way: A person called like me was arrested in Macedonia on the basis of that judgement, bearing the same name and surname as I bear it. After that, Croatian media obtained a statement of the Judge Mile Bilic, who tried president of Serbian Krajina, prime minister, commander of the SVK, and the spokesperson of the Main Staff, who handed down 20 years of prison, in his account. The whole trial took 50 minutes. And as it's stated in that judgement: 45 witnesses were examined; 200 records were also examined; prosecutor's closing remarks and the defence counsel's closing remarks were heard. So far, nobody has ever mentioned this judgement anywhere, and that dubious honour goes to Mr. Harmon. I don't know whether Mr. Harmon knows about the nature and character of this judgement and how it was delivered. And this is something that Your Honours can verify very easily. This is what I had to say. And thank you very much, Your Honours, for allowing me to say it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Novakovic. Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, for the record, the judgement of -- conviction against Mr. Novakovic is dated the 28th of February, 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Sir, I want to turn your attention to Pauk.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If we could have D164 on the monitor, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: General Novakovic, I'm going to request your assistance in this. You have used the pen that is in front of you, and you know how to mark this map. What I'm interested in is could you just circle the area that was involved in Operation Pauk. I see we have -- oh, there we go, we erased it.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could this be marked as Prosecution's next in order, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P2926.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could I have Prosecution Exhibit 1853 on the monitor, please. And I'm interested in page 3 of the English and page 2 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, just -- has P2926 been captured? Because I saw it getting erased. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It has been.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you -- while we're waiting for these images to appear, General Novakovic, can you tell us what the purpose of the Pauk operation was?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I could understand it, the purpose of Operation Spider, or Pauk, was for the refugees from the territory of Western Bosnia who found themselves in the territory of the RSK in Kordun and fighters who were loyal to Alija Izetbegovic [sic] who fled, together with their families, for them to return home. This, how I understood it, was the main purpose and goal of that operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Are you asserting, sir, that the Operation Pauk was a humanitarian operation?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First and foremost of a humanitarian nature, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could we take a look at this document I've asked to be pulled up on the monitor. And I want to direct your attention, sir, to the portion -- let's see if I have the correct page on this for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could we scroll up, please, on that -- down, please, on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I see Mr. Lukic is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Perisic prompted me to highlight an error in transcript. Page 67 [as interpreted], line 10, when he explained the nature -- purpose of the Operation Pauk. And when he mentioned forces loyal to, he should explain to whom they were loyal.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I will examine the witness in due course on that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, the witness said they were loyal to Alija Izetbegovic. And I think the correct reference is page 76, not 67, as it was interpreted.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. I accept that's an error, Your Honour, and it should be -- I can ask the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Sir, in your answer you said that "... the purpose of Operation ... Pauk, was for the refugees from the territory of Western Bosnia who found themselves in the territory of the RSK in Kordun and fighters who were loyal to Alija Izetbegovic ..." Did you mean that the people who were in Kordun were fighters who were loyal to Alija Izetbegovic or did you mean someone else?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. Fikret Abdic of course. It's a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for correcting that mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you to counsel for bringing it to my attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Sir, if we can go back to this -- the B/C/S document, I'm interested in page 2 of the Serbian document. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Is this page 2 on this monitor yet? I can't -- it is. All right. I don't know if it is, Your Honour. I want to be able to locate for the witness the portion I want to direct his attention to, and I'm having difficulty locating it myself on the Serbian-language version. I have located it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you see, General Novakovic, at the top of the page it says -- Roman numeral II, it says "combat units"?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, I just want to check and see if this is the right page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No. Could I go back one page in English. Thank you. So, Your Honours, also directing Your Honours' attention to Roman numeral II, it's about -- a little past halfway down the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Novakovic, this is a document that says: "The VRSK and the VJ" --

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. It's the fourth paragraph down for you, sir. It should be the fourth paragraph down. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could we go back to the top of this document in the Serbian language.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you see Roman numeral II at the top?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Does that say "combat units"?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, do you see a paragraph that says: "The VRSK and the VJ representatives held three meetings with AP ZB President Fikret Abdic in Velika Kladusa, with the aim of preparing an offensive activity by the AP ZB forces to regain seized territory and liberate new territories ending at the Cazin area." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that, Mr. Harmon, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, General Novakovic, the 5th Corps of the ABiH posed a lethal threat on your southern flanks, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lethal threat, that would be picturesque description. I could not deem it as such. It was a threat. It was dangerous. I can concede that. But I'm not sure whether you are asking me questions about Operation Pauk, or Spider, or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm asking you about the 5th Corps and whether the 5th Corps that was operating in the area that you circled for us on D164 posed a military threat to your southern flanks, to the RSK. Did it or did it not?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It posed a threat, and it was active in an area which was broader than that which are encircled. You asked me to encircle the area where Operation Pauk took place. You did not ask me, Mr. Harmon, to delineate the zone or area of responsibility of the 5th Corps. I did not do that. I did what you asked me to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Did the 5th Corps operate in the area that you circled?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in that area as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And did the 5th Corps operate -- that operated in that area pose a threat to your southern flanks?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could pose a threat, and let's say that it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And did the 5th Corps also pose a military threat to the forces of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course it did pose a threat. The two were at war, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, can you please tell me, sir, what were the advantages to the SVK if they reinstalled Fikret Abdic and his forces in the area that you circled?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the moment when this document was created, Mr. Harmon, Fikret Abdic's forces were in the area that I encircled. Please, let's not get mixed up on that. Let's avoid any confusion here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let's try to be perfectly clear, General Novakovic. Operation Pauk was directed against the 5th Corps for the purpose of reinstalling Fikret Abdic in the area that you circled; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order for people to return and in order to prevent problems that had been created in Kordun, Mr. Harmon, and for us to have a friendly rear, that was our position, Mr. Harmon, and those are the facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So you wanted to reinstall Fikret Abdic along your rear flanks because you would have an ally -- or at least a -- not -- you wouldn't have an enemy that could potentially threaten the RSK's existence. Do you agree with that proposition or not?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree, Mr. Harmon. But that was not our only interest, and it was not as it is described in this document here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. My question then originally was -- I had you what the military advantages were to the RSK if Fikret Abdic was in -- reinstalled. What were the military advantages to the SVK -- to the VRS? I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, I believe that we are again talking at cross-purposes. Things have gotten so mixed up that the Trial Chamber will never understand the gist of this situation. At that time, Fikret Abdic's forces were in the territory, and there was nowhere for them to turn because they were already there. At the moment on -- when I saw the document on the 20th of August, this year - and this document is dated June - after the 20th of August our biggest security problem is -- the security problem in Kordun was the number of citizens of Kordun, the overpopulation, and all the problems that arose from that fact. And that actually became the main problem. We're talking about different periods. We were not in a position to return them anywhere. They were already there. And once they left, their number one was this; number two is -- also what you are referring to and that is friends in our rear flanks rather than enemies. And that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, let's approach it slightly differently, General Novakovic. What military forces were used in Operation Pauk? Were SVK forces used in Operation Pauk?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, partially, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: How many SVK forces were used, and what units were used in Operation Pauk?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the Serbian Krajina army, support came in the form of two or three artillery batteries -- not at all times, mind you. Also, the forces of the border detachment that normally manned the front line facing the 5th Corps. And as the front line was moved forward, those forces moved there own front lines and kept on manning the front line and defence lines facing the 5th Corps. Sometimes even the Western Bosnian forces, or rather, forces loyal to Fikret Abdic advanced across their lines. Those were the participants on the side where Operation Pauk took place, and those were support forces from the Serbian Army of Krajina. In order to enforce the 21st border detachment, occasionally forces up to the strength of a company were brought in from all the three brigades of the 21st Corps, and that is also true.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What forces of the VRS were involved in Operation Pauk?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: VRS forces which were engaged, but not throughout the entire duration of the operation, were forces up to the strength of one battalion at most. Mr. Harmon, I'm not talking about forces which were engaged in a battle with the 5th Corps normally; I'm just talking about Operation Pauk in the zone that I marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Sir, what forces from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia MUP were involved in Operation Pauk?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say that those men that had arrived from Serbia were members of the federal MUP or the MUP of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. I never heard that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you ever hear that MUP units or MUP personnel were engaged in Operation Pauk?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as individuals. But I was told that they were volunteers from Serbia. I don't know who they were. I never inspected their IDs or official documents, if they had them at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you ever meet with Jovica Stanisic in respect of Operation Pauk?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Where did you meet with him?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Kordun.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you meet with him in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in Belgrade too.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Who did you meet him with when you went to Belgrade to meet him in respect of Operation Pauk?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember, sir. There were many such meetings involving different people, so it's very hard for me to remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What Federal Republic of Yugoslavia members did you meet with in respect of Operation Pauk while you were involved in the operation?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I was involved in the operation or while I was army commander?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: While you were involved in Operation Pauk.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met with Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: On how many occasions?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now let me just return to the forces of the SVK because you described them a moment ago and I want to ask you specifically. Were forces of the 21st Corps involved in Operation Pauk?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said that, and I can repeat it if --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No, there's no reason to repeat it. Were forces of the 11th Corps used -- of the SVK used in Operation Pauk?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Occasionally, for certain short periods, units ranging in strength from a company to two companies were brought in.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were VJ forces used in Operation Pauk?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Beside the forces of the VRS, the SVK, and the FRY MUP, can you tell us what other military forces were used in Operation Pauk? Fikret Abdic's forces is another element --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think the witness said those were volunteers, not the FRY MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's what he said, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We also failed to address Fikret Abdic's forces, sir. They were obviously involved in, obviously, Operation Pauk. Were there any other forces used in Operation Pauk beside the ones we have been exploring?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fikret Abdic's forces were the main part of the forces. The others were just occasional participants. The other forces -- I don't know. Nothing comes to mind. Maybe you can jog my memory, and if I can remember anything, I'm certainly going to confirm what you asked me. There's no reason for me to hide anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, this would be an appropriate time to take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And do you want to jog his memory on this last point before we take a break?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Once again, we haven't finished with you, Mr. Novakovic. We'll start again tomorrow at 9.00 in the morning. Again, you may not discuss the case with anybody. Court adjourned to 9.00 Friday morning in Courtroom II.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 3rd day of September, 2010, at 9.00 a.m.
